# Abstract

`visStatistics` provides a workflow for routine two-variable frequentist inference in R.
Given two vectors, `visstat()` first dispatches by variable classes, factor levels, sample sizes, expected cell counts, and explicit user options.

Its assumption-driven branch concerns tests of central tendency for a numeric response grouped by a factor.
There, in the default setting, sample size and residual diagnostics from a fitted linear model choose between rank-based and mean-based tests and, within the latter, between equal-variance and Welch-type variants.

The output is deliberately visual: diagnostic plots are shown together with assumption-test p-values, the selected test, effect size, and post-hoc results where applicable.
This shifts attention from ad-hoc test selection to visual diagnostic assessment and statistical interpretation.

The automated workflow of `visStatistics` is particularly suited for server-side R applications, where users select variables through a web interface and receive a complete visual statistical analysis.
It also supports time-constrained work such as statistical consulting, where less time spent on test selection leaves more room for interpretation.

# Introduction

In the frequentist tradition, most routine data analyses reduce to a comparatively small set of inferential frameworks, including group comparisons, regression models and contingency-table analyses [@Fritz:2012; @Hayat:2017; @Sato:2017; @Brodeur:2020]; their correct use depends on assumptions that are often checked informally or not at all [@Hoekstra:2012, @Shatz:2024].
`visStatistics` targets this gap by making routine frequentist test selection assumption-aware, visual, and reproducible.
Rather than requiring users to choose the test function first, `visstat()` starts from two variables and routes common two-variable settings through a fixed decision workflow.
It selects a test from the variable classes, distributional assumptions, sample size, and expected cell counts; displays the diagnostics that led to the selected route; and returns an R object whose `print()` and `summary()` methods expose the complete test results, including the reported effect size.
The scripted workflow is well suited for browser-based applications where sensitive data (such as highly confidential medical records) are stored securely on a server and cannot be directly accessed by users.
This approach was already successfully applied to develop a medical scoring tool [@Bijlenga:2017].

# Packages with related scope

For group comparisons, packages with related scope include `compareGroups` [@Subirana:2014], `boxTest` [@Sau:2025], `autotestR` [@Garcia:2026], and `automatedtests` [@Zeevat:2025].
`compareGroups` is primarily designed for bivariate descriptive tables and reports.
`boxTest` covers only the two-group numeric-response case.
`autotestR` provides automated recommendations for t-tests, ANOVA and correlation.
`automatedtests` provides the broadest coverage among these packages, including one-sample, paired, repeated-measures, regression, correlation, and contingency-table cases.

For tests within the general linear-model framework like Student's t-test or Fisher's ANOVA and linear regression, the normality assumption concerns the model residual errors (each observation minus its predicted value), not the raw data; the belief that the raw data must be normal is a widespread myth [@Kery:2003].
Yet none of these packages checks normality on the residuals of the fitted linear model.
Instead, `autotestR` and `boxTest` test the response separately within groups, whereas `automatedtests` and `compareGroups` test the response variable as a whole, ignoring the grouping.

Among the reviewed automated test-selection packages, `visStatistics` is thus the only one that bases the central-tendency route on explicit residual diagnostics from the common linear model rather than on marginal or groupwise normality checks.
The package is deliberately limited to common two-variable settings in which the route can be visualised and audited: residual-based diagnostics for the linear-model branches, the selected test, full test statistics, effect size, result plots, and post-hoc comparisons where required.

Note that packages such as `rstatix` [@Kassambara:2025], `ggstatsplot` [@Patil:2021], and, in Python, `pingouin` [@Vallat:2018] provide individual diagnostic and test functions but leave the actual test choice to the user rather than automating it.



# Purpose of the vignette

The purpose of this vignette is three-fold: On the one hand it explains the decision logic of `visstat()` (Section \@ref(sec:decision)) and illustrates it on examples for each branch of the decision logic (Section \@ref(sec:examples)).
It further quantifies, by Monte Carlo simulation (Section \@ref(sec:simulation-results)), the Type I error and power of the automated Route 1 gating against fixed mean-based and fixed rank-based defaults.
On the other hand its Appendices serve as reference of all implemented tests, correlations and effect-sizes, so that the user easily understands the output without having to consult the code or literature.

# Package overview

`visStatistics` [@Schilling:2026] is available on [CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=visStatistics) as the latest stable release.
This article refers to the latest development state in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/shhschilling/visStatistics) (<https://github.com/shhschilling/visStatistics>), which may include minor changes between CRAN submissions.

Given two input vectors `x` and `y` of class `"numeric"`, `"integer"`, or `"factor"`, its main function `visstat()` can be called in two equivalent forms:

``` r
# Recommended form:
visstat(x, y)

# Formula interface:
visstat(y ~ x, data = dataframe)
```

An exemplary function call is

```{r npk, fig.show='hide', results='hide'}
# Standardised form
visstat(npk$block, npk$yield)
```

From this single entry point, the package automatically selects among the implemented hypothesis tests,

`t.test()`, `wilcox.test()`, `aov()`, `oneway.test()`, `kruskal.test()`, `chisq.test()`, `fisher.test()`, `lm()`.

The underlying selection algorithm is detailed in Section \@ref(sec:decision).

Among the returned components, `visstat()` reports the p-value of the selected test and an `effect_size` field (Section \@ref(sec:effect-size)).

Unless stated otherwise, R function names for selected tests refer to functions from the `stats` package distributed with R [@R:2026].

To reduce dependencies on other packages, `visStatistics` implements `levene.test()` for the variance gate in grouped mean-based tests (Eq. \@ref(eq:levene-f)), `bp.test()` for regression diagnostics (Eq. \@ref(eq:breusch-pagan-bp)), and `games.howell()` for Welch-ANOVA post-hoc comparisons using the Welch statistic (Eq. \@ref(eq:welch-t)).

Definitions of all implemented test statistics, rank-correlation coefficients, and effect sizes are given in Appendices \@ref(sec:tests)--\@ref(sec:rank-correlations).


## The `visstat` methods {#sec:visstat-methods}


Objects returned by `visstat()` are of class `"visstat"` and support the S3 methods `print()`, `summary()`, and `plot()`.
Each is demonstrated on a worked object in Section \@ref(sec:anova-plantgrowth).

- `print()` lists the returned components.
- `summary()` prints the full returned object, including assumption tests, post-hoc comparisons, confidence level, and `effect_size` where available.
- `plot()` lists the available plots by default; with `which`, it either replays a captured plot (in an interactive R session) or reports the selected saved file path.


### Saved graphics

When `visstat()` is called with `graphicsoutput` specified, `plot()` lists the generated file paths instead.
All generated graphics can be saved in any file format supported by `Cairo()` [@Urbanek:2025], including "png", "jpeg", "pdf", "svg", "ps", and "tiff".
If `plotName` is provided, the main result plot uses this name.
The assumption-diagnostic plot adds the prefix `"glm_assumptions_"`.
If `plotName` is not provided, file names are generated from the selected plot type and the input variable names.

# Decision logic {#sec:decision}

The decision logic of `visstat()` is layered: The general branching, summarised in Figure \@ref(fig:overview), is driven by the `class` and number of factor levels of its input vectors.

Only for a numeric response with a categorical predictor, the selection among tests of central tendency further depends residual diagnostics from a fitted linear model (Section \@ref(sec:route-1)).

## Top-level routing by input class {#sec:top-level}






The main branching logic consists of four default routes summarised in Figure \@ref(fig:overview).

- Route 1. Numeric responses with categorical predictors enter the central-tendency branch detailed in Section \@ref(sec:route-1).
- Route 2. Ordered categorical responses with categorical predictors follow the non-parametric Wilcoxon or Kruskal--Wallis route (Section \@ref(sec:route-2)).
- Route 3. Two numeric variables enter simple linear regression (Section \@ref(sec:route-3)).
- Route 4. Two unordered factors enter the proportion-comparison branch (Section \@ref(sec:route-4)).

Rank-correlation analyses are optional user-requested alternatives for ordered--ordered and numeric--numeric inputs.
They are reached only when `correlation = TRUE` is set explicitly.

```{r overview, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Overview of all implemented tests selected based on input class.", fig.alt="Flowchart showing all implemented statistical tests organised by the class of the input vectors."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/overview.png")
```

## General linear model framework {#sec:glm}

Student's t-test, Fisher's ANOVA (both belonging to Route 1) and simple linear regression (in Route 3) are special cases of the general linear model framework [@Thompson:2015] and share the same model assumptions: the expected value of the response is a linear function of the predictors, the error terms are mutually independent and normally distributed with expectation 0, and the error variance is constant.

Residuals are the empirical realisations of these error terms.
To check whether the residuals fulfil the linear model assumptions, `visstat()` both *vis*ualises (see Section \@ref(sec:graphical)) and formally assesses the normality and homoscedasticity of the residuals by assumption tests (see Section \@ref(sec:assumption-tests)) for tests belonging to Route 1 and Route 3.
Note that only in Route 1, $p$-values derived from these assumption tests influence the test selection (Section \@ref(sec:route-1)).

Below, Section \@ref(sec:math-glm) formally defines the general linear model framework in the context of the implemented tests.

### General linear model definition {#sec:math-glm}

In the general linear model, a response $Y$ is modelled as a linear combination of $k-1$ predictors $x_j$.
The general linear model for observation $i,\;i = 1, \ldots, N$ is then

\begin{equation}
(\#eq:glm)
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots +
   \beta_{k-1} x_{i,k-1} + \varepsilon_i,
\end{equation}

where $Y_i$ is the response for observation $i$, $x_{ij}$ is the value of predictor $j$ for observation $i$, $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{k-1}$ are the $k$ parameters, and $\varepsilon_i$ is the model error term assumed to be independent and normally distributed with expectation 0 and constant variance $\sigma^2$, in short $$\varepsilon_i \sim \mathscr{N}(0, \sigma^2),
\quad\mathrm{mutually\; independent}. $$

The variance $\sigma^2$ represents the variation of the data about the regression, $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$, as both the (unknown) model parameters and predictors are not random.

From Eq.
\@ref(eq:glm), the special cases used by `visstat()` follow from the predictor structure:

**Student's t-test** uses one binary indicator variable $x_{i1}$, with $x_{i1}=0$ for group 1 and $x_{i1}=1$ for group 2.
Let $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ denote the expected mean values in the two population groups.
For the expected values of the response, we then obtain $$E(Y_i \mid x_{i1}=0)=\mu_1=\beta_0$$ for group 1 and $$E(Y_i \mid x_{i1}=1)=\mu_2=\beta_0+\beta_1$$ for group 2.
Testing $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is therefore equivalent to testing $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$.

**Fisher's ANOVA** generalises this coding to $k-1$ binary indicator variables for $k$ groups; testing $H_0: \beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_{k-1} = 0$ is equivalent to testing equality of $k$ group population means.

**Simple linear regression** uses one continuous predictor; $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ examines whether a linear relationship exists.

#### Residuals

The observable counterparts of the model error terms $\varepsilon_i$ in Eq.
\@ref(eq:glm) are the residuals.
After fitting the data with the corresponding linear model, the raw residual is

\begin{equation}
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i,
(\#eq:raw-residual)
\end{equation}

where $y_i$ is the observed value and $\hat{y}_i$ the fitted value for observation $i$;

\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_i = b_0 + b_1 x_{i1} + \cdots +
   b_{k-1} x_{i,k-1}
\end{equation} with the estimated values $b_0, b_1, \ldots, b_{k-1}$ for the unknown model parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{k-1}$.

The magnitude of the raw residuals depends on the unknown model error variance $\sigma^2$, which gets estimated by the square of the standard error $SE_\text{res}^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} e_i^2}{N-k}$.
Dividing the raw residuals by the standard error we obtain the z-residual

\begin{equation}
z_i = \frac{e_i}{SE_\text{res}},
(\#eq:z-residual)
\end{equation}

which facilitates model comparison across different scales of the raw data.

##### Standardised residuals

The residual standard error $SE_\text{res}$ is a *global* estimate for the unknown $\sigma$, but not an estimate for the variance of the *individual* residual $\operatorname{Var}(e_i)$.
It can be shown [@Cook:1982, p. 14] that

\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Var}(e_i)=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii}),
(\#eq:var-leverage)
\end{equation}

where the leverage $h_{ii}$ of observation $i$ is the $i$-th diagonal element of the $N \times N$ hat matrix $\mathbf{H}$, which maps the observed values onto the fitted values [@Cook:1982, p. 11].
$h_{ii}$ measures how strongly observation $i$'s own observed value $y_i$ influences its fitted value $\hat{y}_i$.

Equation \@ref(eq:var-leverage) shows that the raw residuals carry an unequal, leverage-dependent variance even when the errors are homoscedastic: observations with higher leverage have a smaller individual residual variance.
Internally studentised ("standardised") residuals correct for this artefact.
Dividing $e_i$ by its estimated individual standard error gives

\begin{equation}
r_i =\frac{e_i}{\sqrt{ SE_\text{res}^2\,(1-h_{ii})}}=
\frac{z_i}{\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}.
(\#eq:standardised)
\end{equation}

### General linear model assumption tests {#sec:assumption-tests}

**Normality tests** The normality of the standardised residuals is formally assessed using both the Shapiro--Wilk (SW) test [@Shapiro:1965; @Royston:1982; @Royston:1995] (`shapiro.test()`; Eq.
\@ref(eq:shapiro-w)) and the Anderson--Darling test [@Anderson:1952] (`ad.test()`; Eq.
\@ref(eq:anderson-a2)).
These tests offer complementary strengths: Anderson--Darling is highly sensitive to tail deviations in larger samples [@Yap:2011], while Shapiro--Wilk generally exhibits greater power across non-normal distributions in small samples.
The Shapiro--Wilk test is used as the normality gate in the automated test selection (Section \@ref(sec:route-1)).



**Homoscedasticity tests** For grouped central-tendency analyses, variance homogeneity of standardised residuals [@Cook:1982] is assessed using the package-implemented mean-centred Levene test [@Levene:1960] (`levene.test()`; Eq.
\@ref(eq:levene-f)) and Bartlett's test [@Bartlett:1937] (`bartlett.test()`; Eq.
\@ref(eq:bartlett-k2)).

Bartlett's test is powerful under normality but sensitive to non-normality;
Levene-type tests trade some power for greater robustness when distributions
depart from normality [@Brown:1974].




Therefore, Levene's test is used as the variance gate in the automated workflow.

For simple linear regression, group-based variance tests are not applicable.
There, `visStatistics` uses its package implementation `bp.test()` of the Breusch--Pagan test [@Breusch:1979] (Eq. \@ref(eq:breusch-pagan-bp)) on raw residuals [@Schutzenmeister:2012].

### Visualisation of the assumptions of the general linear model {#sec:graphical}

Since algorithmic logic based on p-values of assumption tests cannot replace expert visual judgment, `visstat()` *vis*ualises the assumptions of the underlying linear model for the selection of tests of central tendency (Route 1) and for simple linear regression (`correlation = FALSE`) (Route 3).


For numeric responses with categorical predictors (Route 1), the diagnostic panel displays the residual histogram, the normal Q--Q plot with simultaneous tolerance band (STB) and point-wise tolerance band (TB) [@Schutzenmeister:2012], and the absolute standardised residuals $|r_i|$ (Eq. \@ref(eq:standardised)) by group.
The last panel shows whether residual spread is comparable across factor levels, the pattern assessed formally by the Levene (Eq. \@ref(eq:levene-f)) and Bartlett (Eq. \@ref(eq:bartlett-k2)) variance checks.

For Route 3 (simple linear regression), the first two diagnostic panels follow the layout of Route 1, whereas the third panels displays z-scaled residuals versus fitted values.



The first row of the outer tile of the diagnostic plot reports p-values of residual-normality checks with the Shapiro--Wilk test and Anderson--Darling tests.
The second row reports p-values of variance checks: Levene and Bartlett for grouped central-tendency analyses, or Breusch--Pagan for simple regression.

Note that among the displayed assumption tests, only the Shapiro--Wilk and Levene test results enter automated routing, and only in the central-tendency branch (see Section \@ref(sec:route-1)).
Anderson--Darling, Bartlett, and Breusch--Pagan are diagnostic output only.


The Route 1 and Route 3 diagnostic-panel designs are illustrated in the examples in Figures \@ref(fig:welch-anova-example), left, and \@ref(fig:regression-example), left.



## Route-specific decision rules {#sec:route-rules}

The general branching is driven by input class and factor levels (Section \@ref(sec:top-level)).
Within the selected route, additional rules determine the selected test and output; these route-specific rules are detailed below.

### Route 1: Numeric response, categorical predictor {#sec:route-1}

A numeric response with a categorical predictor with $k$ "levels" (in the following "groups") asks whether the response differs between groups.

Figure \@ref(fig:decision-tree) expands the default routing logic for tests of central tendencies.

```{r decision-tree, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Decision tree for the default Route 1 test selection (group\\_test = NULL). Shapiro--Wilk on model residuals determines whether the route remains mean-based or switches to rank-based tests; the Levene test then selects equal-variance or Welch-type procedures.", fig.alt="Decision tree for the default Route 1 test selection among Welch t-test, Student t-test, Wilcoxon, Fisher ANOVA, Welch ANOVA, and Kruskal-Wallis tests, based on the Shapiro-Wilk test on model residuals and the Levene test for variance homogeneity."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/decision_tree.png")
```


A linear model of Eq.
\@ref(eq:glm) is fitted between the numeric response and the categorical predictor, and the model residuals of Eq.
\@ref(eq:raw-residual) are extracted.

In the default setting (`group_test = NULL`), Route 1 uses the displayed residual diagnostics of the Shapiro--Wilk (SW) and Levene test (L) [@Levene:1960] as automatic gates:

The Shapiro--Wilk (SW) normality test functions as the residual-normality gate, because simulation studies report high power for small to moderate sample sizes [@Razali:2011].^[R's `shapiro.test()` is defined only for sample sizes between 3 and 5000. Above that limit `visstat()` uses the Anderson--Darling test (Eq. \@ref(eq:anderson-a2)), which has no upper sample-size limit, as the residual-normality gate instead.]

If the SW-test rejects residual normality ($p_\text{SW} \le \alpha$), robust non-parametric tests are selected: `wilcox.test()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:wilcoxon-w)) for two groups, or `kruskal.test()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:kruskal-h)) followed by Holm-adjusted `pairwise.wilcox.test()` for more than two groups.

If residual normality is not rejected, variance homogeneity the mean-centred Levene test (L) [@Levene:1960] (Eq. \@ref(eq:levene-f)) gates the variance assessment:

For homoscedastic data ($p_\text{L} > \alpha$), `t.test(var.equal = TRUE)` (Eq. \@ref(eq:student-t)) is applied for two groups, or Fisher's `aov()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:fisher-f)) for more than two groups.
For heteroscedastic data ($p_\text{L} \le \alpha$), Welch's `t.test()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:welch-t)) is applied for two groups, or Welch's `oneway.test()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:welch-f)) for more than two groups.

A type I error of the Levene test merely routes homoscedastic data to Welch's t-test or Welch's one-way ANOVA, which lose only negligible power when variances are in fact equal simple sizes are large.
[@Rasch:2011; @Delacre:2019].

Independent of assumption testing, the user can enforce group mean comparisons by the option `group_test = welch` which defaults to Welch variants of the t-test (`t.test()`) and ANOVA (`oneway.test()`), otherwise the option `group_test = rank`switches to the non-parametric alternatives `wilcox.test()` and `kruskal.test()`.

The rational for the automated gating, and the mean- and rank based alternatives and the limitations of each approach are discussed in section \@ref(sec:simulation-results).








#### Post-hoc tests {.unnumbered}

ANOVA, Welch ANOVA, and Kruskal--Wallis are omnibus tests: a significant test result tells us that *some* group differs, but not which.

To identify the differing pairs, `visstat()` tests all pairwise comparisons among the factor levels, defining a family of tests.
Because the three omnibus tests rest on different assumptions, each branch uses a matching post-hoc procedure:

- `TukeyHSD()` (Eq. \@ref(eq:tukey-hsd-q)) after `aov()` controls the family-wise error rate through the studentised range distribution under a common-variance assumption.

- `games.howell()` after `oneway.test()` uses the Welch statistic (Eq. \@ref(eq:welch-t)) with separate variance estimates and Welch-adjusted degrees of freedom for each pair, making it the appropriate post-hoc procedure for the heteroscedastic Welch branch.

- `pairwise.wilcox.test(p.adjust.method = "holm")` after `kruskal.test()` uses Holm's step-down adjustment for the pairwise Wilcoxon tests in the Kruskal--Wallis branch.

The graphical results panel of these omnibus tests consists of box plots (see examples in Section \@ref(sec:examples-route1)) enriched with significance letters to visualise the post-hoc analysis: Pairs whose adjusted post-hoc $p$-value falls below $\alpha$ are marked with different green significance letters below the box plots; pairs sharing a letter are not significantly different.






### Route 2: Ordered response {#sec:route-2}

An ordered categorical response with a categorical predictor or ordered categorical predictor is treated as a rank-based group comparison.
The ordered response is converted to integer level codes and analysed with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for two groups or the Kruskal--Wallis test for more than two groups.

### Route 3: Numeric response, numeric predictor {#sec:route-3}

Two numeric variables ask whether a numeric response changes with a numeric predictor.
By default, `visstat()` fits a simple linear regression (Eq. \@ref(eq:simple-regression-fit)).
and the diagnostic panel described in Section \@ref(sec:graphical) is displayed.
If general linear model assumptions are violated, the corresponding p-values trigger warnings and recommendations, but no automatic model replacement.
The regression output is shown in Section \@ref(sec:lin-reg).

### Route 4: Two unordered factors {#sec:route-4}

Two unordered factors ask whether two categorical variables are independent.
`visstat()` uses Pearson's $\chi^2$ test or Fisher's exact test, depending on expected cell counts following Cochran's rule [@Cochran:1954]: the $\chi^2$ approximation is used if no expected cell count is less than 1 and no more than 20% of cells have expected counts below 5.
Yates' continuity correction is applied by default to $2 \times 2$ tables when the $\chi^2$ approximation is used.

### Optional rank-correlation mode {#sec:rank-correlation-mode}

The four routes above describe the default, automatic test selection behaviour.
For ordered--ordered and numeric--numeric input vectors, the user can instead request a rank-correlation analysis by setting `correlation = TRUE`.

Both optional analyses test monotone association and are computed by `cor.test()`: Kendall's $\tau_b$ (Eq. \@ref(eq:kendall-tau-b)) with `method = "kendall", exact = FALSE` for two ordered variables, and Spearman's $\rho$ (Eq. \@ref(eq:spearman-rho)) with `method = "spearman"` for two numeric variables.
Kendall's $\tau_b$ corrects for ties present with few ordered levels [@Agresti:2010; @Xu:2013].

Note that for numeric--numeric input, Pearson correlation is not implemented as a separate optional mode as in simple linear regression with an intercept, the two-sided test of zero slope and the two-sided Pearson correlation test return the same $p$-value.



# Route 1 simulations {#sec:simulation-results}

Route 1 can answer two different questions. Mean-based tests — Student's t-test,
Fisher's ANOVA, and their Welch variants — test equality of population means
[@Welch:1951; @Rasch:2011; @Delacre:2019]. Rank-based tests — the Wilcoxon rank-sum
test and the Kruskal--Wallis test — test a rank-based distributional target that
coincides with a location shift only under additional shape assumptions
[@Fagerland:2009]. `visstat()` commits to one of the two on every call. Section
\@ref(sec:route-1) described how: in the default setting `group_test = NULL` the
residual diagnostics decide, whereas the two overrides `group_test = "welch"` and
`group_test = "rank"` fix the choice in advance. The simulations below quantify what
each of these three settings costs.

Under `group_test = "welch"` the analysis remains mean-based and uses Welch's t-test
for two groups and Welch's one-way ANOVA for more (`W`). A Welch default avoids the
Type I error introduced by preliminary variance tests
[@Moser:1992; @Zimmerman:2004; @Rochon:2012] and gives directly interpretable
estimates and confidence intervals [@Harrell:2026], but it can be weak for strongly
skewed small samples [@Blanca:2017; @Fagerland:2012] and can answer the wrong
scientific question when the mean lies in a long tail
[@Fagerland:2009; @Harrell:2026]. The cost of defaulting to Welch-type mean
comparisons is small in the equal-variance balanced case: Welch's t-test then
coincides with Student's t-test, and for more than two balanced groups the Welch ANOVA
statistic converges to Fisher's statistic with a relative difference of order $n^{-1}$
(Eqs. \@ref(eq:welch-student-pooled) and \@ref(eq:welch-anova-equal-var-reduction)).

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) allows the formal assessment of residual normality
assumed in Welch tests to be bypassed in large samples: by the CLT, the sampling
distribution of the group means approaches normality as the group sizes grow,
regardless of the shape of the underlying distribution, so that in large enough
samples a rejected residual-normality test no longer necessarily threatens the
validity of the mean-based routes, Fisher/Student and Welch alike. This raises the
practical question of what should count as a "large enough" sample. The answer depends
on the shape of the underlying distribution, especially skewness and tail weight, here
parametrised by excess kurtosis [@Lumley:2002], and the simulations below give it for
the shapes and designs simulated.

Under `group_test = "rank"` the analysis remains rank-based and uses `wilcox.test()`
for two groups and `kruskal.test()` for more (`KW`). This reduces distributional
assumptions and can be efficient under skew
[@Bridge:1999; @Harrell:2026; @Franc:2025], but changes the estimand
[@Fagerland:2009] and gives less direct mean-scale interpretation [@Harrell:2026].

The default `group_test = NULL` lets residual shape decide instead.
The Shapiro--Wilk test on the standardised residuals of the fitted general linear
model routes rejected residual normality to `wilcox.test()` or `kruskal.test()`, and
retained residual normality to the mean-based branch, where the Levene test then
selects between the equal-variance tests (Student's t-test, Fisher's ANOVA; `F`) and
the Welch variants (`SW+L`). Test selection based on assumption tests suffers from the
fact that all hypothesis tests are underpowered in smaller samples, and thus often
fail to detect assumption violations, and overpowered in large samples
[@Ghasemi:2012; @Fagerland:2012; @Shatz:2024], so that in larger samples even mildly
skewed data are sent to the rank-based route.

The simulations display the fixed tests and the routed procedures side by side: fixed
Fisher/Student (`F`), fixed Welch (`W`), a Levene gate between them (`L`), fixed
Kruskal--Wallis (`KW`), a Shapiro--Wilk gate between `W` and `KW` (`SW`), and the full
Shapiro--Wilk plus Levene gate (`SW+L`), which selects `F` or `W` within the
mean-based branch and `KW` otherwise. Of these, `W`, `KW` and `SW+L` are the three
implemented options; `F`, `L` and `SW` are references. `L` isolates the variance gate
for mean comparison and `SW` isolates the residual-shape gate, so the difference
between `SW` and `SW+L` measures what the second gate contributes.

The aim of the four-group simulations is not to re-establish the robustness evidence for Fisher's
ANOVA under homoscedasticity and non-normality [@Blanca:2017] or for Welch's ANOVA
under heterogeneous variances [@Delacre:2019]. Instead they show for  which
combinations of sample size, skewness and excess kurtosis the displayed residual
diagnostics route from the mean-based branch to rank-based tests, when the Levene gate
keeps Fisher/Student or selects a Welch variant, and where each strategy leaves the
robustness bounds used below.

 Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI)
adapts the three-group zero-effect one-way ANOVA setting of Blanca et al.
[@Blanca:2017] to four Route 1 groups with identical distributions, and
Figure \@ref(fig:route1-unequal-typeI) varies the group standard deviations and the
sample-size pairings as in Delacre et al. [@Delacre:2019].

Each cell uses $B = 50{,}000$ Monte Carlo replications. For an estimated rejection
probability $\hat{p}$ the Monte Carlo standard error is
$SE_{\mathrm{MC}}=\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/B}$ [@Koehler:2009], about 0.10 percentage
points at $\hat{p}=0.05$ and at most 0.22 percentage points at $\hat{p}=0.50$.
Five input distributions are used throughout, generated with Fleishman's polynomial
transformation $Y = a + bX + cX^2 + dX^3$, where $X \sim N(0,1)$ and the coefficients
set mean 0, variance 1, and the target skewness and excess kurtosis [@Fleishman:1978].
Their (skewness, excess kurtosis) pairs are $(0,0)$, $(0,6)$, $(0.5,1)$, $(1,1.6)$ and
$(2,6.6)$; the first two are symmetric.
Balanced designs use $\mathbf n=(n,n,n,n)$ with $n \in \{10,20,50,100\}$; unbalanced
designs use $\mathbf n=\bar n\cdot(0.5,0.8,1.2,1.5)$, giving group sizes
$(5,8,12,15)$, $(10,16,24,30)$, $(25,40,60,75)$ and $(50,80,120,150)$ for
$\bar n \in \{10,20,50,100\}$. Equal-SD designs use $\mathbf s=(1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0)$;
unequal-SD designs use $\mathbf s=(1.0,1.3,1.7,2.2)$, and in the unbalanced case this
vector is either kept, so that larger groups carry larger SDs, or reversed to
$\mathbf s=(2.2,1.7,1.3,1.0)$, so that larger groups carry smaller SDs.
The simulation scripts and the saved Monte Carlo output are shipped with the package;
`system.file("simulations", package = "visStatistics")` returns their directory, whose
`README.md` documents how to rebuild the three figures from the saved results and how
to re-run the simulations themselves.

An empirical rate is reported as non-robust when it leaves Bradley's liberal bounds of
$[2.5\%, 7.5\%]$ at $\alpha = 5\%$ [@Bradley:1978]. This is a reporting convention
without principled status — Bradley's own argument is that no fixed interval defines
robustness — and it is used here only so that the same threshold is applied in every
figure. In Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI) the colour scale is capped at
7.5%, so any exceedance would be visible at a glance; none occurs.

Three rules apply when reading the heatmaps.

1. Rows `F`, `W` and `L` always report the rejection rate of a mean-based test, in the simulations of  Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI))  and Figure \@ref(fig:route1-unequal-typeI) the population means are in set ups equal they are Type I error rates in every cell.
2. Rows `KW` (shown only in Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI)), `SW` and `SW+L`
   report the rate of whichever test was finally selected, so their interpretation
   differs between the two figures. In Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI) the
   four groups share one distribution, so the equal-means null and the rank-based null
   are true simultaneously and these rows are Type I error rates in every cell. In
   Figure \@ref(fig:route1-unequal-typeI) they are Type I error rates only in the first
   two columns, whose input distributions are symmetric: multiplying a symmetric
   distribution by a group-specific SD leaves group means, medians and mean ranks
   equal. In the three skewed columns the same rescaling shifts group medians and mean
   ranks, so only the share of replications routed to a mean-based test — the
   percentages after the bar other than the `KW` one — remains a Type I error rate,
   while the rank-routed share is a rejection rate against a hypothesis that is false.
3. The percentages after the vertical bar are route probabilities, not rejection
   rates: `F` and `W` for the `L` row, `W` and `KW` for the `SW` row, and `F`, `W` and
   `KW` for the `SW+L` row. They identify which test produced the rate to their left.

## Type I error simulations: equal means, equal ranks, balanced or unbalanced group sizes

Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI) shows in panel (A) the five input
distributions shared by all four groups, in panel (B) a balanced design and in
panel (C) the unbalanced one, each with rows ordered from top to bottom by increasing
$n$ and $\bar n$ respectively.

Because all four groups are identically distributed, the equal-means null and the
rank-based null are simultaneously true, and by rule 2 every row of both heatmaps is a
Type I error rate. This is therefore the clean Type I check of the automated routes:
a switch to the rank-based branch cannot change the truth status of the hypothesis
tested.

```{r simulation-captions, include=FALSE}
cap_route1_identical_typeI <- paste(
 "Route 1 Type I simulation under identical distributions and identical",
 "means, with group mean 0 and SD 1 in all four groups.",
 "(A) input distributions.",
 "(B) balanced design with group sizes $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4 = n$ ",
 "listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100. ",
 "(C) Unbalanced design with group sizes $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4 = \\bar{n} \\cdot ",
 "(0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 1.5)$ with $\\bar{n} \\in \\{10, 20, 50, 100\\}$ ",
 "listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100, rounded up to the next integer. The heatmaps in",
 "(B) and (C) report final-test rejection rates at $\\alpha = 5\\%$.",
 " Cells for SW and SW+L",
 "additionally report the route split. In (A), dashed lines",
 "mark means and dotted lines mark medians. The index i = 1, ..., 4",
 "denotes groups; $\\bar n$ denotes the target mean group size for unbalanced",
 "designs. All heatmap numbers are percentages; the first value is the",
 "final-test rejection rate, and gated rows list route splits after |."
)

cap_route1_unequal_typeI <- paste(
 "Route 1 simulation: identical means and unequal distributions;",
 "$\\mathrm{mean}_i = 0$ ($i = 1, \\ldots, 4$).",
 "Route 1 equal-means simulation with varied group standard deviations",
 "and sample-size pairings. (A) input distributions. (B) balanced design,",
 "listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100.",
 "(C) unbalanced design with larger $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4$ paired with larger SD,",
 "with rows listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100.",
 "(D) unbalanced design with larger $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4$ paired with smaller SD,",
 "with rows listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100.",
 "F, W, and L are mean-null tests; SW and SW+L report final-test",
 "rejection after possible routing to Kruskal--Wallis. In (A), dashed",
 "lines mark means and dotted lines mark medians. The",
 "index i = 1, ..., 4 denotes groups; $\\bar n$ denotes the target mean",
 "group size for unbalanced designs, listed from top to bottom as 10, 20, 50, 100. All heatmap numbers are percentages;",
 "the first value is the final-test rejection rate, and gated rows list",
 "route splits after |."
)
```

```{r route1-identical-typeI, echo=FALSE, fig.cap=cap_route1_identical_typeI, out.width="95%"}
knitr::include_graphics(
 "figures/route1_identical_distributions_typeI_with_kw_fleishman_B50000.png"
)
```

No cell of either heatmap leaves Bradley's bounds. Across both designs, all five input
distributions and all four sample sizes, `F` ranges from 4.43% to 5.18%, `L` from
4.32% to 5.33%, `KW` from 4.28% to 5.06%, `SW` from 4.24% to 5.57% and `SW+L` from
4.53% to 5.71%. The widest spread belongs to fixed Welch, from 3.63% in the balanced
design at $n=10$ for the symmetric heavy-tailed input to 6.80% in the unbalanced
design at $\bar n=10$ and $\bar n=20$ for the most skewed input. The robustness of
Fisher's ANOVA to non-normality under homoscedasticity established by Blanca et al.
[@Blanca:2017] therefore extends, in this grid, to both Welch variants, to the rank
test and to both gated procedures; adding the Levene gate to `SW` never moves the rate
by more than 0.92 percentage points.

This is also where the price of the Welch default can be read against its algebraic
size. For four balanced homoscedastic groups, $F/F_W = 1+3/[5(n-1)]$
(Eq. \@ref(eq:welch-anova-four-groups)), so the Fisher and Welch statistics differ by
6.7% at $n=10$ and by 0.6% at $n=100$. In the normal column of panel (B) the
corresponding rejection rates differ by at most 0.06 percentage points at every $n$:
a difference of several per cent in the test statistic is invisible in the decision it
produces.

The route probabilities show how the two gates behave when their assumptions hold and
when they are mildly violated. Under the normal input the Shapiro--Wilk gate sends
4.67%, 5.01%, 4.85% and 5.06% of replications to the rank branch at $n=10, 20, 50$ and
$100$ — it does not drift with sample size — and `SW+L` selects Fisher's ANOVA in
89.01% to 90.09% of replications throughout. Under mild skewness the same gate drifts
strongly: for the $(0.5,1)$ input the rank route rises from 16.95% at $n=10$ to
31.79%, 64.12% and 90.24%, and for the $(2,6.6)$ input it is 87.57% at $n=10$ and
100% from $n=50$ on. The Levene gate drifts in the same direction. This is the
underpowered-in-small-samples and overpowered-in-large-samples behaviour of assumption
tests, visible here as route probabilities rather than as an argument from the
literature: in large samples even a mild shape departure is routed to the rank branch,
at a Type I cost that is nil in this design.

## Equal means, unequal ranks

In Figure \@ref(fig:route1-unequal-typeI) all four group means remain zero and only the
group standard deviations change. Panel (B) is the balanced design, panel (C) the
unbalanced design in which larger groups carry larger SDs, and panel (D) the unbalanced
design in which larger groups carry smaller SDs.

```{r route1-unequal-typeI, echo=FALSE, fig.cap=cap_route1_unequal_typeI, out.width="85%"}
knitr::include_graphics(
 "figures/route1_equal_means_unequal_distributions_fleishman_B50000.png"
)
```

One route probability in this figure needs explanation, because it is otherwise
paradoxical: in the normal column, where every group is exactly normal, the
Shapiro--Wilk gate still routes 13.31%, 22.78%, 45.04% and 72.47% of replications to
the rank branch in panel (D). The gate is applied to the standardised residuals of the
common fitted model, which divides all groups by a single residual standard error. If
the group variances differ, the pooled residuals are a scale mixture of normal
distributions and therefore leptokurtic, so residual normality is correctly rejected
with increasing frequency as $n$ grows even though no group is non-normal. Under
heteroscedasticity the residual-shape gate thus responds to the variance
heterogeneity, not only to the shape of the input distributions.

## Where Bradley's bounds are exceeded

Two of the five designs produce no exceedance at all: both equal-SD designs of
Figure \@ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI), as reported above, and the balanced
unequal-SD design of panel (B), where `F` reaches at most 6.19%, `W` at most 6.91% and
`L` at most 6.76%, in each case at $n=10$ under the $(2,6.6)$ input.
Heteroscedasticity alone, at equal group sizes, is thus not enough to make any of the
six strategies non-robust in this grid, which is the numerical counterpart of the
recommendation to prefer balanced designs [@Delacre:2019].

Every exceedance comes from an unbalanced design, and its direction is set by which
groups carry the large SD. Under equal means and unequal variances,
$E[MS_\text{within}] = \sum_i (n_i-1)\sigma_i^2/(N-k)$ weights each group variance by
its own degrees of freedom, whereas
$E[MS_\text{between}] = \sum_i \sigma_i^2(1-n_i/N)/(k-1)$ weights it by $1-n_i/N$.
Assigning the large SD to the small group therefore enlarges the numerator and
shrinks the denominator of Fisher's $F$, and the reverse assignment does the opposite;
both weights are ratios, so the distortion does not diminish as the sample sizes grow
[@Glass:1972]. Panel (D) is the first case: `F` rejects between 11.84% and 13.11% at
every input distribution and at every $\bar n$ from 10 to 100, with no tendency to
decrease. Panel (C) is the reverse: `F` is conservative throughout, between 2.55% and
3.11%, and falls below Bradley's lower bound at $\bar n=10$ and $\bar n=20$ for the
symmetric heavy-tailed input, at 2.40% and 2.38%. Fisher's ANOVA and Student's t-test
are therefore not weakly but systematically affected by the direction of the imbalance
under unequal variances, in both directions.

Fixed Welch leaves Bradley's bounds in only two cells of the entire grid, both in
panel (D) and both at the most extreme input $(2,6.6)$: 10.83% at $\bar n=10$ and
9.09% at $\bar n=20$. At $\bar n=50$ it is back inside at 7.22%, and at $\bar n=100$
at 6.26%. Delacre et al. [@Delacre:2019] established that the empirical Type I error
of Welch's one-way ANOVA — whose two-group special case is Welch's t-test — remained
within Bradley's bounds across their simulated non-normal distributions, which
included skewed chi-square cases with skewness 2 and excess kurtosis 6, close to the
most extreme input used here, and a symmetric mixed-normal case in which 90% of the
observations are drawn from one normal distribution and 10% from a second normal
distribution with the same mean but four times the standard deviation
[@Delacre:2019code]. That mixture has excess kurtosis 9.7, and is therefore
heavier-tailed than any input simulated here. They
caution that under skewness this robustness requires about 50 observations per group
for up to four groups and about 100 observations per group for more than four groups,
holding the sizes of $k-1$ groups fixed and perturbing only the last. Our design
perturbs all four group sizes simultaneously, so the two thresholds are not directly
comparable: at $\bar n=100$ every group exceeds 50 and Welch is robust, but already at
$\bar n=50$, with groups $(25,40,60,75)$, it is robust as well. The present results
are therefore consistent with their recommendation without being more demanding than
it, and they identify the one setting in which fixed Welch is not sufficient: skewness
2 with excess kurtosis 6.6 at a smallest group of 5 or 10 observations.

The Levene-gated mean route `L` leaves Bradley's bounds in six cells, all in panel (D)
and all at small samples: 9.87%, 9.21%, 9.51% and 9.96% at $\bar n=10$ for the
$(0,0)$, $(0.5,1)$, $(1,1.6)$ and $(2,6.6)$ inputs, and 7.73% and 8.88% at
$\bar n=20$ for $(1,1.6)$ and $(2,6.6)$. It is inside the bounds for every input from
$\bar n=50$ on. The reason is visible in its own route split: in the balanced
unequal-SD design the Levene gate still selects Fisher in 57.33% of replications at
$n=10$ and in 22.53% at $n=20$, but in 0.32% at $n=50$ and in 0.00% at $n=100$. The
Levene mean route thus improves on fixed Fisher/Student in the hardest cells without
reaching Bradley's bounds there: where the variance pretest is underpowered it passes
heteroscedastic data to Fisher and inherits Fisher's bias, and where it is powerful it
selects Welch and becomes redundant with a fixed Welch default
[@Moser:1992; @Zimmerman:2004; @Rochon:2012].

The default `SW+L` inherits both liabilities, and this is the honest price of keeping
Fisher's ANOVA and Student's t-test reachable by automated gating. In the two
symmetric columns of panel (D) — where, by rule 2, the reported rate is a Type I error
rate for both estimands, so no change of hypothesis can excuse it — `SW+L` leaves
Bradley's bounds in six of eight cells: 10.14% and 8.22% at $\bar n=10$, 7.83% at
$\bar n=20$, 7.58% at $\bar n=50$, and 8.07% and 7.76% at $\bar n=100$. Two unrelated
mechanisms act at opposite ends of the sample-size range. At $\bar n=10$ and
$\bar n=20$ the Levene gate is too weak: it routes 45.53% and 19.62% of replications
to Fisher's ANOVA, whose rate in this design is 13%, which is why `SW+L` (10.14%) is
worse there than `SW` (6.47%) and than `W` (5.96%). At $\bar n=50$ and $\bar n=100$
the Levene gate has become irrelevant, the Shapiro--Wilk gate routes 45.04% and 72.47%
of replications to the rank branch, and `SW+L` coincides with `SW` and inherits the
rank test's own sensitivity to unequal variances at unequal group sizes
[@Zimmerman:2004]. Fixed Welch stays inside Bradley's bounds in all eight of these
cells, between 3.96% and 5.96%.

## Type II error (power) simulations

The power simulation uses the same five input distributions and adds ordered location
shifts across the four groups. It uses balanced groups with equal SD, so $n_i=n$ and
$\mathrm{SD}_i=1$ for $i=1,\ldots,4$, and group means are shifted by
$0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75$ SD. Rejection rates are shown for $n=10$ to $n=100$. The
question the figure answers is what the full `SW+L` default costs relative to `SW`,
that is what the second gate contributes once the shape gate has acted.

```{r route1-power, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7.8, fig.cap="Route 1 power simulation with Fleishman input distributions. (A) Input distributions with group mean and median reference lines. (B) Simulated rejection rates for the six testing strategies."}
knitr::include_graphics(
 "figures/fleishman_4groups_power.png"
)
```

Under the normal input the six strategies are indistinguishable at every $n$: at
$n=10$ they lie between 23.04% (`KW`) and 26.36% (`SW+L`), at $n=20$ between 48.35%
and 51.54%, and at $n=50$ between 90.63% and 92.06%. As skewness and tail weight
increase, the rank branch gains: at $n=10$ under the $(2,6.6)$ input `KW` rejects
43.00% against 29.62% for `F` and 31.62% for `W`, and at $n=20$ 78.46% against 54.19%
and 55.75%. Because the Shapiro--Wilk gate routes an increasing share of these
replications to the rank branch, `SW` and `SW+L` follow `KW` rather than the
mean-based tests in the skewed columns; the inset route percentages make that transfer
explicit. At $n=100$ all strategies exceed 99.7% and the comparison is uninformative.

The isolated contribution of the Levene gate is negligible over the whole power grid.
`SW+L` is never below `SW` by more than 0.002 percentage points, exceeds it by at most
2.25 percentage points, and the median difference across the twenty
distribution-by-sample-size cells is 0.004 percentage points. The second gate
therefore changes which mean-based test is reported, and the route display, but not
whether the omnibus null is rejected.

## What the simulations establish

Read strictly as an equal-means procedure, Route 1 is best served by
`group_test = "welch"`: fixed Welch is the only mean-based strategy that stays within
Bradley's bounds in all but two of the 100 equal-means cells, it loses no measurable
power where its assumptions are met, and its algebraic distance from Student's t-test
and Fisher's ANOVA under equal variances is $O(n^{-1})$. Read as a procedure that is
allowed to use input shape as a method switch, `SW` is the simpler automatic route,
and the default `SW+L` buys the same switch while preserving the Fisher/Student branch
of the general linear model when its two displayed assumptions pass. `group_test =
"rank"` is the fixed rank-based choice, but under skewed unequal-SD inputs it answers a
different question.

The simulations therefore do not show that `SW+L` is the best equal-means procedure.
They show its price and its benefit. The price is paid twice in the unbalanced design
whose smallest group carries the largest SD: under skewness the reported rate is
increasingly that of a rank test after the hypothesis has changed, and even under
symmetry the procedure is Type I non-robust there, through the weak variance gate at
small samples and through the rank branch at large ones. The benefit is that the
switch is visible and diagnostic-driven: Fisher's ANOVA or Student's t-test is used
only when both displayed general-linear-model assumptions pass, a Welch variant when
only homoscedasticity fails, and a rank test when residual normality fails, with the
route percentages in the figures documenting each of these decisions directly.


# Reported p-values and effect sizes `effect_size()` {#sec:effect-size}

The selected test output includes the p-value quantifying evidence against the null hypothesis and a complimentary `effect_size` estimate describing the magnitude of the selected comparison, association, or model fit on the scale
defined in Appendix \@ref(sec:effect-size) [@Fritz:2012; @Levine:2002].
While p-values strongly affected by sample size, effect-size, estimates are intended to support comparisons across studies regardless of sample size [@Levine:2002]. Effect size is therefore an important determinant of power or required sample size or both [@Cohen:2013; page 10].




The effect size takes the value zero when the null hypothesis is true and some other, test- specific non-zero value when the null hypothesis is false, it is an an index of degree of departure from the null hypothesis [@Cohen:2013; page 10]



To avoid additional package dependencies, `effect_size()` extracts, where possible, the effect sizes from base R `stats` output, Otherwise it implements the remaining formulae internally.

The following tables summarises the statistical analysis with their respective effect sizes and formulae.
